courses.title: Stoicism
courses.description: A guided reading of Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius and the early Stoic account of what is up to us, how impressions work, and why preferred indifferents are not goods.

lessons.title: What Is Within Our Control
lessons.body:
Epictetus opens the Enchiridion with a division: some things are up to us, and some are not. Judgement, impulse, desire and aversion belong to the first group. Body, property, reputation and office belong to the second. The course takes this as a working map, not as a claim that later Stoics all used the same list.

The practical question is what happens when we treat an external as if it were ours to command. Anxiety, anger and flattery often start there. A promotion, an illness or another person's praise can still matter; the mistake is to locate a good life in their arrival.

Try the distinction on a small case. You can prepare an argument carefully. You cannot guarantee the room will agree. The first is a field for training. The second is a preferred outcome, not a proof that you failed as a rational agent.

lessons.title: Impressions and Assent
lessons.body:
For Epictetus, an impression arrives before the verdict. A slight, a rumour or a sudden pain presents itself as already judged: this is an outrage; this must be feared. The discipline is to pause before assent, and to ask what the impression actually shows.

Assent is not the same as suppressing feeling. A Stoic account can admit that the body startles. The ethical claim is about the second movement: whether we add the story that the world has injured our good.

Keep this separate from a later, popular slogan that Stoicism means having no emotions. The classroom question is narrower: which judgements turn a first impression into a lasting passion, and which withhold that extra claim.

lessons.title: Preferred Indifferents
lessons.body:
Early Stoic ethics treats virtue as the only good and vice as the only evil. Health, wealth and political standing are 'indifferents': they do not make a life good or bad by themselves. Some of them are still preferred. A rational agent may select health over illness without calling health a moral good.

The distinction matters because it blocks two easy readings. One says the Stoic must refuse medicine or money. The other says that once we prefer health, we have smuggled an external good back in. The course keeps the technical pair: select and reject among indifferents, while locating praise and blame in character.

Marcus Aurelius often writes as if court life were a field of such selections. Read those passages as exercises in not confusing office with virtue, not as a demand to leave public life.

courses.title: Song-Ming Confucianism
courses.description: From Zhu Xi's investigation of things to Wang Yangming's liangzhi: how Song and Ming thinkers rebuilt Confucian self-cultivation after the Buddhist and Daoist centuries.

lessons.title: Li, Qi and the Song Revival
lessons.body:
Song Confucians inherited a canon and a problem. After centuries in which Buddhist and Daoist vocabularies had organised elite learning, how could the Classics again explain mind, nature and political order? Zhou Dunyi, the Cheng brothers and Zhu Xi answered by talking about li (pattern or principle) and qi (psychophysical stuff).

Li is not a separate ghostly object. In this classroom account, it is the intelligible order that can be traced in a plant, a family relation or a ritual. Qi is what makes that order concrete, uneven and changeable. Human nature can then be discussed as li present in a particular endowment of qi.

The useful question is not “Is this Western metaphysics?” but “What does this pair let a reader do with the Great Learning and the Mencius?” The course treats the pair as a teaching tool of the Song revival, not as the only way Chinese thought ever named the world.

lessons.title: Investigating Things
lessons.body:
Zhu Xi reads the Great Learning's gewu — often translated 'investigate things' — as a long discipline. One extends knowledge by attending to pattern in affairs and texts, not by a single flash. The commentary tradition makes this a curriculum: read, compare, correct bias, return to the matter at hand.

Critics already in the Song and Yuan worried that gewu could become bookish delay. The course presents Zhu's own warning that investigation without sincerity is empty, and the later complaint that sincerity without investigation is blind.

A classroom test: take a dispute in a household or an office. What would it mean to 'investigate' it in Zhu's sense — to look for the pattern of roles and claims — rather than to collect more gossip?

lessons.title: Wang Yangming and Liangzhi
lessons.body:
Wang Yangming argues that the highest good is not reached by stacking external investigations. Liangzhi — innate moral knowing — is already present when we recognise a child about to fall into a well, to use Mencius' example. The work is to refuse the selfish thought that covers that knowing.

His slogan of the unity of knowledge and action is easy to flatten into 'just do it'. In the Instructions for Practical Living, knowing that is not enacted is not yet knowledge in the moral sense. Sitting still and calling it insight is one of his targets; so is reciting Zhu while remaining unmoved.

Keep the two programmes in view. Zhu offers an extended ladder of study. Wang offers a diagnosis of delay. The course does not ask you to pick a winner on the first reading; it asks you to see what each thinker thought the other had missed.

lessons.title: Community Compact and Cultivation
lessons.body:
Song-Ming self-cultivation was not only inward. Community compacts, academy rules and family rituals were ways of making li visible in a place. Wang's followers and Zhu's school both wrote about local order, though they disagreed about where correction should start.

Read a compact as a pedagogical text: it names faults, praise, and the person who may speak. That is a theory of how shame and encouragement work in a village, not a modern constitution.

The closing question of the course is modest. After li/qi, gewu and liangzhi, what kind of public practice would still count as Confucian cultivation rather than private mood work?

courses.title: History of Science
courses.description: How instruments, correspondence networks and arguments about error turned local crafts into public knowledge — from early modern observatories to the modern laboratory.

lessons.title: What Counts as a Scientific Revolution
lessons.body:
The phrase 'scientific revolution' is a historian's tool, not a date stamped on the seventeenth century. Some narratives centre Copernicus, Galileo and Newton. Others ask what changed in workshops, courts and print shops so that a new claim could travel as knowledge rather than as a local craft secret.

Thomas Kuhn's Structure of Scientific Revolutions made 'paradigm' a household word and also a trap. This lesson uses it sparingly: as a reminder that training, instruments and puzzles hang together, not as a law that science jumps only by rupture.

The classroom question is concrete. When a table of observations disagrees with a respected scheme, what counts as a decisive anomaly, and who is allowed to say so? That is already a historical question about institutions, not only a logical one about evidence.

lessons.title: Instruments and Invisible Colleges
lessons.body:
A telescope, an air-pump or a precision balance does not speak by itself. Someone must build it, trust its scale, and write so that a reader elsewhere can imagine the trial. Early modern 'invisible colleges' and later societies organised that trust: letters, witnesses, and rules about who may repeat an experiment.

Robert Boyle's air-pump controversies are a standard case because they show apparatus, rhetoric and gentlemanly credit moving together. The point is not to mock the rhetoric. It is to see why a public of readers needed a style that claimed anyone could, in principle, see the same thing.

Try a modern parallel with care. A shared dataset and a methods section are descendants of this problem. They are not proof that the seventeenth century was already a modern lab.

lessons.title: Error, Calibration and Trust
lessons.body:
Measurement error is not only a formula. Historians of observatories and surveys have shown how 'enough precision' is negotiated: against the cost of instruments, the weather, and the political need for a boundary or a nautical table.

Calibration is a social practice. A standard metre, a clock, or a spectroscopic line has to be carried, copied and believed. When two stations disagree, the fight is often about which instrument drifted, not about an abstract method.

The course closes on a modest claim. A history of science that only lists discoveries misses the work that makes a number public. A history that only talks about power misses why some procedures still constrain what a community can say.

courses.title: Greek Tragedy
courses.description: Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides on the civic stage: chorus, recognition, and the gods as problems for the democratic city rather than as costume.

lessons.title: The Civic Stage
lessons.body:
Athenian tragedy was performed at the City Dionysia before a civic audience, with a chorus that is neither a narrator from nowhere nor a simple stand-in for 'the people'. Masks, metre and the restricted number of speaking actors shape what a story can do in a day.

The course starts here so that later talk of fate or psychology has a place. A recognition scene works differently when the city is watching a myth it already knows, and when the chorus can delay, question or refuse the hero's language.

Keep tourism at a distance. We do not recover the festival by listing gods. We recover a public art that made old houses — Atreus, Labdacus, Theseus — answerable in a democratic present.

lessons.title: Aeschylus and the Law
lessons.body:
The Oresteia moves from household blood to a civic court. The Furies are not a special effect; they are a claim that some injuries cannot be paid in the old language of revenge. Athena's tribunal does not erase them. It offers them a seat in the city.

Read the trilogy as an argument about institutions, not as a simple progress tale from darkness to light. The chorus of the Agamemnon already knows how praise and fear work in a victorious city. The Eumenides asks what a court can hold that a family cannot.

A classroom caution: 'the birth of law' is too smooth. Aeschylus stages a compromise that still needs ritual, persuasion and the threat of what the city almost became.

lessons.title: Sophocles and Recognition
lessons.body:
Aristotle's anagnorisis — recognition — is easiest to see in Oedipus Tyrannus, but Sophocles uses the turn in more than one play. A character discovers a kinship, a crime, or a limit that speech had been circling. The audience is often ahead; the drama is in how the city on stage absorbs the knowledge.

Antigone is not only a clash of 'state versus individual'. Creon and Antigone each claim a law. The chorus has to live with both claims after the bodies are on the ground. That is a civic problem, not a verdict to take home as a slogan.

Try reading a recognition scene aloud with the choral ode that follows. The ode often generalises just when the house needed a particular name. That friction is part of Sophocles' design.

lessons.title: Euripides and the Gods
lessons.body:
Euripides lets gods open and close plays in ways that unsettle a tidy moral. The Bacchae does not ask whether Dionysus 'exists'. It asks what a city does with a god it has refused to recognise, and what kind of seeing Pentheus is offered as punishment.

Medea and Hippolytus raise a different pressure: passion, oath and reputation inside a household that the city still has to judge. Divine frames do not cancel the human argument; they make the costs harder to moralise away.

The course does not settle whether Euripides is pious, ironic or both. It asks you to track who is allowed to speak for a god, and what the chorus can no longer sing after that speech.

courses.title: Climate Systems
courses.description: Earth's energy balance, circulation and feedbacks, and how paleoclimate records plus modern observations constrain what a 'climate system' can do.

lessons.title: Energy Balance of the Earth
lessons.body:
A climate system is first an accounting problem. Incoming shortwave radiation is scattered, absorbed and re-emitted. The planetary energy balance says that, over a suitable average, outgoing longwave radiation must match the absorbed solar input. Greenhouse gases change the height and temperature from which the planet can radiate that longwave flux.

This lesson stays with the budget before policy language. Albedo, the diurnal cycle and the difference between surface temperature and effective radiating temperature are the working parts. A slogan about 'the atmosphere as a blanket' is allowed only if you can say what the blanket does to the emission height.

A first exercise: if the solar constant and the Bond albedo are given, what effective temperature follows? Then ask what extra story is needed to reach a typical surface temperature. That gap is the greenhouse effect in this course's vocabulary.

lessons.title: Circulation and Feedbacks
lessons.body:
The atmosphere and ocean move heat from the tropics toward the poles. Hadley cells, western boundary currents and the seasonal march of the ITCZ are mechanisms, not wallpaper. They also couple to water vapour, clouds and ice — the feedbacks that decide how a forcing is amplified or damped.

Water-vapour feedback is comparatively robust in this teaching sequence: a warmer column can hold more vapour, and vapour is a greenhouse gas. Cloud feedbacks are not. The course names the uncertainty instead of hiding it. Ice-albedo feedback is clearer on long, polar timescales than in every regional winter.

Keep weather and climate distinct. A circulation regime can shift and still be the same climate in the energy-budget sense. The lesson asks when a shift in a jet or a monsoon is a response to a changed budget, and when it is internal variability.

lessons.title: Paleoclimate and Observation
lessons.body:
Ice cores, marine sediments and tree rings extend the instrumental record. They do not speak in degrees Celsius by themselves. A proxy is a translation, with seasonality, dating error and a calibration that must be argued.

The instrumental era adds a different constraint: radiosondes, satellites and ocean floats. Together they limit the stories one can tell about sensitivity and about whether a forced trend is distinguishable from variability.

The course ends on method, not on a campaign sentence. If two reconstructions disagree, the scientific move is to ask about the proxy, the age model and the spatial coverage — the same habits the history-of-science course named as public knowledge.
